overview.headline: How balanced and unbalanced forces control aircraft motion

keyPoints.point: Simplified motion studies balanced aircraft forces one direction at a time
keyPoints.quote: some of the four forces acting on the aircraft are balanced by other forces and that we are looking at only one force and one direction at a time

keyPoints.point: Cruising airplane sustains constant speed in level flight
keyPoints.quote: an airplane could sustain a constant speed and level flight

keyPoints.point: Unbalanced forces move aircraft toward direction of greater force
keyPoints.quote: If the forces become unbalanced, the aircraft will move in the direction of the greater force.

keyPoints.point: Aircraft acceleration follows mass and net force acting on aircraft
keyPoints.quote: Where a is the acceleration, m is the mass of the aircraft, and F is the net force acting on the aircraft.

keyTerms.gloss: upward force balanced against weight in steady flight
keyTerms.quote: the weight would be balanced by the lift and the drag would be balanced by the thrust.

keyTerms.gloss: downward pull that decreases as fuel burns during cruise
keyTerms.quote: While the weight decreases due to fuel burned, the change is very small relative to the total aircraft weight.

keyTerms.gloss: forward push forming an opposing pair with drag
keyTerms.quote: The net force is the difference between the opposing forces; lift minus weight, or thrust minus drag.

keyTerms.gloss: resistance that will cause slowing when thrust remains constant
keyTerms.quote: And increasing the drag at a constant thrust will cause the plane to slow down:

keyTerms.gloss: acting difference that produces acceleration in aircraft motion
keyTerms.quote: Where a is the acceleration, m is the mass of the aircraft, and F is the net force acting on the aircraft.
